p.title: Identifying hidden coalitions in the US House of Representatives by optimally partitioning signed networks based on generalized balance

ext.title: Identifying hidden coalitions in the US House
ext.document_type: Journal article (open access, CC BY 4.0). Metadata hint verified against the PDF front matter; no correction needed. Received 5 June 2021, accepted 3 September 2021.
ext.coverage: Full text read in two chunks (all 682 text lines, front matter through references and licence block). All 58 annotation items in _annots/a93789ed82c1.json were read; all are Paul Goff highlights on pages 1-8 with empty content (no sticky-note text). Figures and SI tables are referenced but not in the text file, so figure content is taken from captions and prose only. The Supplementary Information is not in the source and was not read.
ext.research_question: (1) Can globally optimal partitions of a signed network into k mutually divisive, internally cohesive clusters (generalized balance / k-clusterability) be computed for realistic social networks? (2) What is the smallest k that minimizes frustrated edges? (3) Does partitioning US House legislators by their signed collaboration and opposition ties fit the chamber better than partitioning by party, and what does the resulting structure say about legislative effectiveness?
ext.theory: Generalized (k-) balance and clusterability theory (Davis 1967; Cartwright and Harary 1976), extending classic structural balance (Heider 1944; Cartwright and Harary 1956). A signed network is k-balanced if its nodes split into k coalitions with positive ties within and negative ties between. Distance from balance is the count of frustrated edges. Coalitions are clusters and need not be cohesive or collaborating (p.5). The political reading is that a third, ideologically fluid splinter coalition may organize the chamber beyond party.
ext.data: Sample: 19 US House networks, one per two-year session, with session start years 1981 through 2017 (the text also says the study covers 1981 to 2018, p.2). Unit: legislator pairs, each edge signed positive (significantly more co-sponsorships than chance) or negative (significantly fewer). About 445 nodes per network (paper: n ~ 445). Edges: 4,954 to 31,936 (p.4). Source: bill co-sponsorship data, bipartite legislator-bill network, then bipartite projection, then signed backbone (p.7). Ideology: 1st-dimension Nokken-Poole scores from Voteview, -1 liberal to +1 conservative, varying by session (p.8). Effectiveness: Center for Effective Lawmaking scores from 15 indicators, normalized to mean 1 per session (p.8). The paper says code and data are public in the SI (p.8).
ext.method:
Two binary linear programs, solved to global optimality with Gurobi 9.1 on a 32-core Windows Server VM (p.4). Eq. (1), the k-partition model: binary x_ic assigns node i to cluster c, and f_ij flags frustrated edges. The objective is the minimum frustrated edges for fixed k, C_k(G). Constraints are O(n^2). Eq. (2), a reformulation of the correlation clustering / clique partitioning model (Demaine et al. 2006) for non-complete graphs: binary y_ij marks same-cluster pairs, with constraints over connected triads T. It returns C(G), the minimum over all k, and k*min. Constraints are O(n^3). Signed networks come from the Stochastic Degree Sequence Model in the R backbone package (v1.5.0), with family-wise error alpha = 0.01 via Holm-Bonferroni (p.7-8). Comparison: frustrated-edge counts for party partitions vs optimal k-partitions for k = 2..7. Then coalition mean legislative effectiveness and median ideology, with 95% CI bands (Fig. 4). Analysis is descriptive and per session, with no regression reported.</method>
<parameter name="identification">None in the causal sense. The design is descriptive. The signed network is inferred from co-sponsorship, and optimal partitions are compared with party partitions on frustrated-edge fit. Coalition effectiveness is compared in descriptive plots with CI bands, with no model controlling for party, majority status or committee assignment. The authors discuss the majority-party effect qualitatively (p.6).
ext.scope: Population: members of the US House of Representatives, sessions starting 1981 through 2017 (text says 1981 to 2018). Institution: the lower chamber only. Era: 1981 to 2018, with contrasts between the 1981-1993 and 2003-2017 sessions (p.5). The optimization methods are general for signed networks up to about 30,000 edges (p.4, p.8). The substantive claims are limited to the House.

key_findings.finding: Globally optimal k-partitions (Eq. 1) and the minimal-k clusterability index (Eq. 2) are computationally feasible for the 19 House networks, up to about 30,000 edges.
key_findings.numbers: Eq. 1 averages 3.3 h; Eq. 2 averages 14 h for networks up to ~30,000 edges. n ~ 445; 4,954 <= m <= 31,936.

key_findings.finding: In every session the party partition leaves more frustrated edges than the optimal 2-partition, which leaves more than the optimal 3-partition. Three coalitions fit the chamber better than two or party.
key_findings.numbers: C_party(G) > C_2(G) > C_3(G) in every session.

key_findings.finding: Beyond k = 3 the frustrated-edge count declines only marginally and then stagnates. For all 19 networks, C(G) = C_k(G) for every k <= 7, so the minimal clusterability index is reached at small k.
The third coalition's size and median ideology vary across sessions, so it is an ideologically fluid group and not a fixed ideological bloc.
key_findings.numbers: Third coalition ranges from 4 members (113th, 2013) to 69 (111th, 2009). Its ideology ranges from very liberal (98th-102nd, 1983-1991) to center-left (103rd, 111th) to center-right (105th-110th, 1997-2007).

key_findings.finding: The third coalition is the most effective coalition in most sessions. Its inclusion explains why the two dominant generalized-balance coalitions are less effective than their party-defined counterparts.
key_findings.numbers: No pooled effect size or test reported; effectiveness is shown as session means with 95% CI bands.

key_findings.finding: Third-coalition effectiveness is anchored by a few very effective members during stable party control. Effectiveness dips during transitions when the majority changes.
key_findings.numbers: 99th-102nd (1985-1990): Pat Williams 4.49, Barney Frank 4.02, Daniel Glickman 3.68. 106th-108th (1999-2004): Christopher Smith 8.44, Bill Young 4.41, Nancy Johnson 2.98. 114th-115th (2015-2018): Edward Royce 5.46, John Katko 5.36, Dave Reichert 2.30.

key_findings.finding: The third coalition has a distinctive sign structure: far more negative (opposition) ties per positive tie, and more of its opposition ties run to co-partisans.
key_findings.numbers: Traditional coalitions: 2.68 negative edges per positive edge. Third coalition: 21.18 (SI Fig. S3). Co-partisan share of negative edges: 8.44% for traditional coalition members, 25.6% for third coalition members.

key_findings.finding: Party, classic balance (k = 2) and generalized balance (k = 3) all show a majority-party effectiveness advantage. The authors attribute this to agenda control and majority vote share. They also say part of the advantage comes from the highly effective third coalition, which is usually ideologically aligned with the majority.
key_findings.numbers: No numerical effect size given for the majority advantage.

key_findings.finding: Party-based coalitions show increasing ideological polarization over time, and classic-balance coalitions look similar. Generalized balance adds a smaller, fluid third group between two diverging dominant coalitions.
key_findings.numbers: No regression or correlation values reported. Descriptive only.

limitations: No dedicated limitations section. In-text caveats: the models can yield multiple optimal solutions, so they do not return a unique partition (p.3-4).

Scale: the models are demonstrated on networks up to about 30,000 edges. The authors call this a minor limitation because many empirical signed networks are sparser, and backbone methods can sparsify dense ones (p.8).
The median ideology of the third coalition is unstable across sessions, so it is not a fixed ideological category (p.7).
Coalition membership 'does not necessarily imply cohesion with other members of the same coalition' (p.5).
The effectiveness comparisons are descriptive plots with 95% CI bands. No controls or inferential tests are reported in the main text (p.6-7).
Signed ties come from a statistical backbone of co-sponsorship, so their validity depends on that inference step (p.7).
measures: Frustrated edges per partition; k-clusterability index C_k(G) for fixed k; C(G) as the minimum over all k; k*min as the smallest k attaining C(G).
Signed co-sponsorship network (SDSM backbone): positive and negative edge counts, and the negative-to-positive ratio per coalition.
Co-partisan share of each member's negative edges.
Ideology: 1st-dimension Nokken-Poole score (Voteview), session-specific, -1 liberal to +1 conservative.
Legislative effectiveness: Center for Effective Lawmaking score (15 indicators, normalized to mean 1 per session), averaged per coalition with 95% CI.

The primary task of legislators is to pass laws, and their ability to do so is referred to as legislative effectiveness. Therefore, we examine the legislative effectiveness of coalitions in the US House of Representatives, again considering coalitions defined from three perspectives.

Coalitions based on political parties (Fig. 4, top panel) illustrate an expected pattern: The majority party is most effective. This occurs not only because the majority party has more votes, but because it controls key procedural details of the chamber.

Coalitions based on generalized balance (Fig. 4, bottom panel) also display a similar pattern, but with important differences. The large liberal coalition is still more effective when Democrats hold the majority, while the large conservative coalition is still more effective when Republicans hold the majority.

rel.summary_md:
Aref and Neal build signed House networks from co-sponsorship for 19 sessions (1981-2017, about 445 members each). They use an SDSM backbone, so an edge is positive when a pair co-sponsors significantly more than chance and negative when significantly less (alpha .01, Holm). They then solve two binary linear programs to global optimality: the minimum frustrated edges for a fixed k, and the smallest k that reaches the overall minimum. In every session the party split leaves more frustrated edges than the optimal 2-partition, and that leaves more than the optimal 3-partition. k*min runs from 3 to 7, but gains past k=3 are small. The third coalition is small (4 to 69 members) and its ideology shifts from session to session. It is the most effective coalition in most sessions on the CEL LES. It also has an unusual sign pattern: 21.18 negative ties per positive tie, against 2.68 for the two main blocs, and 25.6% of its negative ties go to co-partisans, against 8.44%. All of this is descriptive. There are no controls and no causal design.

What this means for the system as built: `fec/network/signed_coalitions.py` cites this paper but works on a different graph. It partitions the LLM-valenced member-mention layer, which mixes House and Senate and is 83% positive, using a heuristic local search capped at k=3. Its stored artifact (2026-07-19) shows a single main bloc plus a 14-member splinter at k=2. At k=3 the third cluster has one member, and frustration barely moves (1040.79 to 1039.79 weighted). So the system has not reproduced the paper's finding and has not tested it. The paper's real substrate, a signed co-sponsorship backbone, is not built in the live code. The June vote backbone threw away exactly the negative ties that define the third coalition. The CEL LES data is already on disk, so a House-only reproduction is cheap. The finding should stay UNVERIFIED until that reproduction runs.

bearings.paper_claim: The k-partition objective minimizes frustrated edges, meaning negative edges inside a cluster plus positive edges between clusters (Eq. 1, giving C_k(G)). Eq. 2 gives the minimum over all k and k*min. Both are solved to global optimality on networks of up to 31,936 edges (Eq. 1 averages 3.3 h, Eq. 2 averages 14 h).
bearings.system_side: Uses the same frustration objective, weighted by |net|. It runs a single-node best-move local search with a party seed plus 60 random restarts, only for k=1..3. The result is an upper bound with no optimality guarantee, and k*min is never searched. The module is a diagnostic: the chain does not consume it, and weekly_refresh runs it after the chain.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The objective transfers directly. The guarantee does not: local search can stop in a local optimum, and the paper's main methodological point is that heuristic partitions are only approximate. At 520 nodes and 7,153 edges the graph is inside the paper's demonstrated scale, so the exact Eq. 1 ILP is feasible here (for example with PuLP/CBC or Gurobi).

bearings.paper_claim: On signed co-sponsorship backbones, House-only and per session, C_party > C_2 > C_3 in all 19 sessions. A distinct third coalition of 4 to 69 members appears. Negative ties are plentiful: 2.68 negative per positive in the traditional coalitions.
bearings.system_side: The signed graph is member_references.json: cross-media mentions, LLM-valenced, with House and Senate mixed (McConnell and Rand Paul appear in the splinter). It has 520 nodes and 7,153 edges, 5,959 positive and 1,194 negative. The stored artifact (data/lobbying/signed_coalitions.json, 2026-07-19) shows weighted F(1)=1092.31, F(2)<=1040.79 (15.31% of total weight) and F(3)<=1039.79. The k=2 result is not bipolar (one bloc plus a 14-member splinter), so the party-recovery check returns None. The k=3 clusters have 506, 13 and 1 members.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence does not carry over. Mention valence measures expressed sentiment, while SDSM signs measure collaboration and avoidance against a degree-preserving null. The system's graph also mixes chambers and pools across Congresses, where the paper is House-only and per session. The system's null third-coalition result says nothing for or against the paper. A test needs a House-only, per-Congress signed co-sponsorship backbone.

bearings.paper_claim: The third coalition is defined by its negative ties: 21.18 negative edges per positive edge, and 25.6% of its negative edges go to co-partisans, against 8.44% for traditional coalition members. Its members are the most effective in most sessions.
bearings.paper_location: p.7 (Results, last paragraph; SI Fig. S3)
bearings.system_side: The June vote backbone was sdsm on member x (vote, side) with alpha .05 BH, and later a party-controlled null. Its negative side was dropped because it 'conflates maverickness', and only cross-party positive ties were kept for Vote Affinity in the Signed Coalitions sheet.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's ties come from co-sponsorship, not votes, so this is not a like-for-like refutation. It does show that same-party negative ties, the 'maverick' signal, are exactly what separates the effective splinter in the House, so dropping them removes the structure the paper finds. This applies only if the vote-backbone negatives behave like co-sponsorship-backbone negatives, which is untested.

bearings.paper_claim: Builds a signed network from the legislator-bill bipartite projection using SDSM, which preserves the expected legislator and bill degree sequences. Positive and negative edges are significant deviations at FWER alpha .01 (Holm-Bonferroni).
bearings.system_side: The engine co-sponsor graph is unsigned, has no negative edges, and is weighted (original 1.0 / regular 0.5, success-weighted, Congress-decayed, 1/sqrt(C)). It is mean-symmetrized for cascades. The holistic_norm config divides by sqrt(Out_u*In_v).
bearings.transfer_conditions: A signed SDSM backbone could be added as a separate diagnostic layer feeding signed_coalitions. It should NOT replace or reweight kernel edges: SDSM is a degree-preserving null, which is a form of per-edge volume normalization, and that proposal was measured and rejected in this project. The paper uses all co-sponsorships, so it does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges.

bearings.paper_claim: Effectiveness is the CEL LES (15 indicators, normalized to mean 1 per session). The paper compares coalition-mean LES with 95% CI bands across party, k=2 and k=3 partitions. The third coalition is the most effective in most sessions, and its effectiveness is anchored by a few members (e.g. Chris Smith 8.44, 106th-108th).
bearings.system_side: lep_criterion.py already loads CEL House and Senate data (93rd-118th) from fec/lep/*.dta, including lesclassic and dwnom1, for a pre-registered convergence look against the blended score.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The LES data needed to reproduce the paper's coalition-effectiveness comparison is already local. A House-only, per-Congress k=3 partition can be joined to lesclassic. The result is descriptive (no controls for majority or chair status, which the paper says drive LES) and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it. Any pooled comparison across sessions must be stratified by majority party.

bearings.paper_claim: The hidden third coalition is highly effective and usually aligned with the majority. The authors credit part of its effectiveness to majority agenda control. Effectiveness drops during majority transitions and rests on a few ultra-effective members.
bearings.system_side: Underdog rank = Intrinsic (0.5 Leg% + 0.5 Centrality%) minus Visibility (0.5 Press% + 0.5 Committee%). No code file is recorded.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper defines its 'hidden' bloc by signed-tie structure, not by low press or committee visibility, and its effectiveness is tied to majority status. That is closer to what the lens subtracts (committee position) than to what it rewards. The conceptual link Paul draws is an analogy and is not evidence for the lens's formula.

bearings.paper_claim: Third-coalition members are ideologically fluid (median from very liberal to center-right across sessions) and effective. The paper does not measure persuadability, vote change or electoral vulnerability.
bearings.system_side: PERS is a fixed inverted-U table over stance tiers (Highly Persuadable 0.65 ... Opponent 0.08; PERS_NONE 0.45).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper gives no support for the inverted-U values or for treating third-coalition or Fitzpatrick-type members as more movable. Ideological fluidity at the coalition level is a property of the session-to-session composition, not of how responsive an individual member is.

gaps_exposed: No signed co-sponsorship backbone exists in the live code. The only signed substrates are the LLM-valenced mention layer and a June vote backbone with its negatives dropped, so the paper's House result has never been tested on a comparable graph.
There is no exact (ILP) partition. The local search returns upper bounds only. k is capped at 3, so k*min (3-7 in the paper) is never estimated, and there is no check for multiple optimal solutions.

Partitions are not per Congress and not per chamber. The paper's result is per session and House-only, and it relies on that time-indexing to show the third coalition's fluidity. This is also Paul's 'no tracking over time' critique, which the system shares.
Coalition membership is not joined to CEL LES, even though the data is on disk at fec/lep. The paper's central effectiveness comparison is reproducible but has not been run.
There is no member-level measure of the share of negative ties that go to co-partisans (25.6% vs 8.44% in the paper). bpf and cooperation_v2 capture only cross-party positive share.

The June decision to drop negative vote-backbone edges as 'maverickness' conflicts with the paper's evidence that co-partisan negative ties mark the effective third coalition (p.7). This is worth recording for Paul. It is not a ruling.

Paul links this paper to competitive-seat money effects (competitiveness-multiplier, D-104..D-108). The paper says nothing about money, PVI or reciprocity and cannot be cited as support. Reciprocity is still not validated.

The system's k=3 'third cluster' (1 member, mention layer, window through 2026-07-19 artifact, denominator 520 members across both chambers) must not be presented as the Aref-Neal third coalition or as a list of effective members. rel.paul_alignment: The summary of the method and findings in Paul's annotation is broadly accurate. Two corrections: the roughly 30,000 figure is edges, not variables, and the method does not 'smooth over' frustrated edges, it counts and minimizes them exactly. He is right that the paper has no path-finding and no tracking against national mood. His reading of the third coalition as responsive or vulnerable swing seats (Fitzpatrick) is his own interpretation. The paper defines the bloc by signed-tie structure and LES, and never measures electoral vulnerability or persuadability. His note is now stale in one important way: it treats the paper as an available 'alternative network layer', but the built layer partitions a different graph (LLM mention valence, both chambers, k<=3 heuristic) and found no meaningful third coalition (one member; frustration changes by under 0.1% of weight from k=2 to k=3). The computational-efficiency point holds. The exact ILP is feasible at Melange's scale and has not been tried.

related.why: The authors' earlier paper. It introduces optimal 2-partitions (the frustration index) on signed political collaboration networks, which this paper extends to k clusters and k*min.

Also builds House co-sponsorship networks and relates them to bill passage and effectiveness. The system's success-weighted co-sponsor edges cite it, so the two papers together cover the unsigned and signed versions of the same substrate.
Gives structural balance and status evidence for signed networks, which bears on whether balance-based partitioning is a reasonable model of signed ties.
Another way to find hidden House structure, through committee-network community detection rather than signed-tie partitioning.
Uses the Volden-Wiseman effectiveness framework that supplies this paper's LES outcome.
Methods for inferring negative ties. Relevant because the system's signed layers either lack negative ties or dropped them, while this paper's third coalition is defined by them.

paul_entries.citation: Aref, Samin, and Zachary P. Neal. “Identifying hidden coalitions in the US House of Representatives by optimally partitioning signed networks based on generalized balance.” *Scientific Reports*, vol. 11, no. 1, 7 Oct. 2021, [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-98139-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-98139-w).
paul_entries.text:
Aref, Samin, and Zachary P. Neal. “Identifying hidden coalitions in the US House of Representatives by optimally partitioning signed networks based on generalized balance.” *Scientific Reports*, vol. 11, no. 1, 7 Oct. 2021, [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-98139-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-98139-w).

This article by Stanford Professors Aref and Neal examines the use of three-cluster partitioned networks to identify hidden and unofficial partnerships and coalitions within the House of Representatives, highlighting highly effective legislative groups and duos whose actions otherwise avoid typical headlines. The two main models utilized are an optimal k-partition and k-clusterability index. These methods, when used in tandem, allow for frustrated edges, a result of at times 30,000 variables, to be smoothed over. This methodology is highly valuable to the present research as it both presents an alternative layer that can be substituted or added into future network models, but more importantly allows for massive sets of data to be made computationally efficient, something that will become necessary as additional pipelines are worked into future models. Additionally, the main finding of this paper was a third general coalition within the House of Representatives, one whose median ideology is highly unstable yet highly effective. This coalition can be seen as the truly vulnerable or responsive seats, those like Brian Fitzpatrick who are forced to swing ideologically toward their constituents because their districts are so competitive. Finally, the fundamental weakness of this article is that there is no path-finding algorithm as of yet, and the authors did not measure the shifts of this coalition over time to see how this coalition's ideology responded to changes in national mood.
